claims.text: The proposed intervention is to introduce a small amount of a refractory element, such as W or Mo, into a high-entropy nanoalloy.
Adding a small amount of W or Mo improves the structural stability of a high-entropy nanoalloy relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without the refractory-element addition.
Adding a small amount of W or Mo improves the chemical stability of a high-entropy nanoalloy relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without the refractory-element addition.
The material before intervention is a high-entropy nanoalloy.
Introducing a refractory element produces grain-boundary strengthening.
The refractory-element intervention slows grain growth.
The refractory-element intervention reduces diffusion rates.
Slower grain growth and lower diffusion rates improve high-temperature stability and resistance to degradation.
The relevant baseline is an otherwise comparable high-entropy nanoalloy without the refractory-element addition.
The predicted benefit should hold over 500–1000 degrees Celsius.
The effectiveness of the intervention may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing conditions.
The hypothesis can be tested by annealing refractory-modified and unmodified alloys at high temperature and comparing their microstructural evolution and mechanical properties.
